title: Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a macroscopic surface that electronically controls the phase of visible light across its aperture, allowing it to point and shape a narrow beam without moving the surface. Light emitted from different positions would interfere constructively in the commanded direction. A larger coherently controlled aperture can produce a tighter beam, provided that phase accuracy and useful optical power are maintained across the surface.

Electronic optical steering already exists. The advance sought here is the simultaneous combination of a centimeter-scale coherent aperture, steering over tens of degrees in two dimensions, high concentration of radiated power in one main lobe, rapid complete beam updates, and practical sustained operation. Aperture size alone would not establish this capability, since the reviewed literature already includes devices exceeding a centimeter in one dimension.

Scope clarification: visible operation remains the defining target because it is part of this concept's identity. Near-infrared implementations are relevant precursors and comparative demonstrations of the same architectural challenges, but would not by themselves complete the visible-light target. A programmable beam-steering aperture also does not automatically provide arbitrary holographic imagery.

significance.text: Achieving these properties together would substantially extend inertialess optical beam control. The direct benefit would be a narrow beam that can be redirected electronically across a wide field while retaining the angular resolution of a large coherent aperture. Electronic phased-array radar provides a useful functional analogy: coordinated phase control changes beam direction without mechanically rotating the aperture. This is an analogy about control architecture, not evidence that optical steering currently requires moving mirrors or that radar engineering transfers directly to optical wavelengths.

Such an aperture could improve lidar scanning, free-space optical links, and controlled laser delivery by combining narrow divergence with fast, reconfigurable pointing. Those applications would still need appropriate light sources, receivers where applicable, calibration, optical power handling, thermal management, and performance under real propagation conditions. Meeting the aperture specification would therefore establish a valuable enabling component rather than a complete application system.

Conditional extensions include meter-scale apertures for tighter long-range beams and more capable projection systems. Scaling from centimeters to meters would require separate evidence that coherence, fabrication, control, efficiency, and thermal performance remain manageable. A centimeter demonstration would not establish those extensions.

Immersive holographic displays share the need to control optical wavefronts over a large space–bandwidth product: enough independently useful spatial information to support both a wide viewing field and a usable viewing region. However, steering one beam does not demonstrate full-parallax imagery, correct occlusion, or video-rate image generation. Display performance is a possible downstream connection with additional requirements, rather than this concept's completion criterion.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is scalable coherent control that preserves aperture, field of view, beam quality, efficiency, and update speed simultaneously. The supplied 2025 review describes coupled tradeoffs among control complexity, speed, array scale, and loss, including the density of driving electronics and the difficulty of implementing a large aperture. Improving one headline specification does not establish that the combined capability has been achieved.

Sampling illustrates the scale of the problem. For a dense periodic array to avoid angular aliasing throughout the full propagating angular region, emitter pitch must be no larger than approximately half the wavelength. At 633 nm, that is 316.5 nm. A uniformly sampled aperture one centimeter wide would consequently have roughly 31,600 emitter positions along each dimension, or about one billion positions for a square two-dimensional array. These are geometric estimates under that sampling assumption, not a requirement for one independent electrical driver at every position.

Half-wavelength spacing is not a universal requirement for every useful steering architecture. Restricted angular coverage can relax sampling constraints, and aperiodic arrays can suppress discrete grating lobes over large fields. However, redistributing unwanted light into a diffuse background can reduce the fraction of power in the desired beam. Architectural reductions in driver count must therefore be assessed alongside their effects on controllability, sidelobes, and main-lobe power.

Concrete engineering barriers include distributing light across a large aperture without excessive loss, maintaining accurate phase relationships, calibrating many interacting controls, integrating sufficiently dense electronics, and sustaining operation within electrical and thermal budgets. Fast individual phase shifters alone do not establish fast settled beam commands across the complete aperture. Likewise, a physically large chip does not establish a large coherent emitting aperture or high useful output power.

current_state.text: Xu, Yuan, Yang, Lu, Chen, and Zhou's review, dated 8 May 2025 in the supplied research, reports photonic-integrated-circuit optical phased arrays with divergence below 1 mrad, scanning speeds above 1 GHz, and array scales reaching 49,152 elements. These figures describe different reported demonstrations; the supplied review does not establish them as simultaneous specifications of one device. Its tables also include apertures exceeding one centimeter in one dimension. Continuing practical lidar challenges include efficiency, point rate, calibration, and the interaction among aperture size, angular coverage, and control complexity.

The retained HTML and PDF extracts of that review are partial and truncated, and the PDF extraction has equation defects. The supplied evidence review nevertheless identifies readable passages supporting the performance records and engineering tradeoffs above. These dated results do not establish whether the complete proposed capability remained undemonstrated on 1 November 2026; no freshness evidence was supplied.

A 2024 Scientific Reports comparison table provides a more qualified picture of optical loss than a single typical range. Ten of its fifteen entries report losses between 8.1 and 15.5 dB, while other entries reach losses as large as 43 dB. An eight-antenna amplified InP device reports +21.5 dB gain. Fiber-coupling losses are excluded, and some output figures specifically describe main-lobe power, so the entries are not interchangeable measures of complete-system efficiency. The table extraction is complete, but the retained material is only part of the parent article and does not independently establish its authorship or exact publication date.

The research notes attribute to Ye, Lian, Chen, and colleagues a 32-channel thin-film lithium-niobate array at 633 nm, with a 40° field, 0.41° divergence in the phased direction, and electro-optic rise and fall edges of 12 ns and 14 ns. They identify an Optics Letters publication dated 1 May 2025, volume 50, pages 3090–3093. No source text was retained for this DOI, so the supplied review could not verify the attribution, date, measurements, or width conventions. The nanosecond edges, if confirmed, would not alone establish complete-aperture command settling. Under a uniform-aperture broadside FWHM model, 0.41° at 633 nm would imply an effective aperture of approximately 0.08 mm, but this is a conditional calculation rather than verification of the reported measurement or physical device size.

The research also identifies an APL Photonics perspective dated 7 May 2026 that reportedly favors monolithic electronic–photonic co-integration as a long-term route to scalable arrays and cautions that proposed remedies may be incompatible across material platforms. No text was retained for this source, and its author list and DOI were not extracted. Those attributed views therefore remain unverified in the supplied record and cannot establish a demonstrated integration solution or the latest state of the field.

Tseng and colleagues' 2024 neural étendue-expansion work reports a 64-fold expansion for natural-image holograms, experimentally expanding field of view eightfold in each direction using a 1K-pixel spatial light modulator. The experimental prototype used a 1 mm eyebox. Larger-display performance using an 8K configuration was simulated. The paper's estimate of more than one billion conventional SLM pixels applies to a target of at least 120° field of view and an eyebox greater than 10 × 10 mm²; it is not a universal pixel requirement for every display architecture.

That display result uses a static learned expander and perceptual optimization rather than demonstrating a billion independently programmable dynamic controls. Its supplement documents temporal averaging, including 20 frames for displayed still images, white balancing, and DC compensation; resolution-scaling analysis includes ideal-device assumptions. The supplied review assessed full extracted article and supplementary text but did not visually inspect the figures, so it did not independently validate image quality. These qualifications limit extrapolation without negating the reported 64-fold result. The demonstration does not supply the proposed centimeter-scale steered aperture.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a visible-light aperture at least one centimeter across in both controlled dimensions should electronically steer a single main lobe, without moving parts, over a specified field spanning tens of degrees in both dimensions. Divergence at the tested directions should be consistent with coherent use of the full aperture, with the aperture illumination and beam-width convention reported. A near-infrared implementation could establish a related engineering milestone, but visible operation would still need demonstration for this concept.
completion_criteria.label: Centimeter-scale visible aperture coherently steers tens of degrees in both dimensions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed beam-quality criterion: at each tested direction, the main lobe should contain more than half of all radiated optical power. The test should define the main-lobe integration boundary, report sidelobes and background radiation, and measure total optical efficiency separately from the fraction of radiated power in the main lobe. Null-defined integration has a precedent in the supplied review, but the majority-power threshold here is a proposal rather than an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Main lobe contains most radiated power at each tested direction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed speed and operating criterion: complete beam commands should settle at a rate of at least 1 kHz while satisfying the beam-quality requirements. Measurements should distinguish phase-shifter transitions from full-aperture settling and sustained usable point rate. The demonstration should report wavelength, continuous optical output, total optical efficiency, electrical power including drivers and calibration, and thermal behavior over a declared continuous operating interval. Practicality should be judged against an explicit lidar or communications operating budget rather than an unspecified claim of low power.
completion_criteria.label: Full-aperture commands settle at ≥1 kHz while satisfying beam-quality requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criterion: publish the aperture geometry, control architecture, calibration procedure, far-field measurement method, power accounting, settling definition, and measurement uncertainties. Repeat measurements across a predefined angular grid, command transitions, operating temperatures, and multiple devices, with independent replication where feasible. Such tests would establish demonstrated angular and operating breadth; they would not prove performance at every possible direction or condition. Meter-scale operation, projection, and immersive displays would each require separate demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Documented measurements repeat across predefined conditions and multiple devices

related_concepts.text: Historical holographic-display item: the research mentions a historical item 7 as an immersive display concept, but its text is absent and it cannot be identified with a supplied roster entry. The relevant overlap is programmable wavefront control and space–bandwidth demand. Full parallax, occlusion, and video-rate imagery add requirements beyond single-beam steering. This historical reference should not be confused with the retained identifier OPT-07.

Roster-based comparison with OPT-06, Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic, and OPT-05, Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue: OPT-07 seeks electronically steerable beams whose divergence is set by the coherent aperture. That is distinct from the super-resolution objective named in OPT-06. Wavefront control could be relevant to imaging systems, but it would not by itself establish cellular imaging through scattering tissue or its video-rate performance. These comparisons are conceptual inferences from the supplied titles, not findings about the detailed designs of those entries.

Roster-based comparison with OPT-03, Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow, and OPT-09, Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages: all involve optical hardware integration, but the target functions differ. OPT-03 concerns an integrated light source; OPT-09 concerns communication energy inside packages; OPT-07 concerns spatial control of radiated light over a macroscopic aperture. Success in source integration or low-energy links would not establish aperture coherence, wide-field steering, or main-lobe power concentration.

Roster-based comparison with OPT-10, Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras: sensitive detection could complement an optical sensing or communications system, while OPT-07 supplies beam control. Detector wavelength, sensitivity, and imaging performance remain separate from emitter-aperture performance, and the short-wave-infrared target does not fulfill OPT-07's visible-light scope.

Roster-based comparison with OPT-01, Cascadable few-photon optical transistor, and OPT-02, Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold: these entries concern few-photon control and quantum-source performance. OPT-07 concerns coherent wavefront control across a large aperture. The shared use of optical arrays or photonic integration does not make deterministic photon generation, few-photon switching, or their loss thresholds completion conditions for this aperture.

Roster-based comparison with OPT-04, Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source, and OPT-08, The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium: coherence and optical fields provide broad conceptual connections, but the supplied titles describe distinct source-generation and nonlinear-interaction goals. Neither establishes macroscopic visible beam steering, and OPT-07 does not require either breakthrough.

change_log.change: Preserved OPT-07 and its title, and made visible operation the defining completion target while retaining near-infrared work as relevant precursor evidence.
change_log.reason: The title specifies visible operation, whereas the original proposal allowed near infrared without resolving that scope difference.

change_log.change: Replaced the mechanical-only premise with an explanation of the combined performance advance over existing electronic optical steering.
change_log.reason: The supplied review documents electronic inertialess steering and dynamic wavefront modulation.

change_log.change: Qualified half-wavelength sampling, calculated the corresponding centimeter-scale emitter count, and distinguished emitter positions from independent control channels.
change_log.reason: The spacing condition applies to dense periodic arrays over unrestricted propagating directions; restricted fields and aperiodic architectures change the tradeoffs.

change_log.change: Removed the asserted general visible-array channel limit and blanket telescope or scanner replacement claim.
change_log.reason: The retained evidence does not establish either generalization, and existing centimeter dimensions show that size alone is insufficient.

change_log.change: Separated the 2025 review's divergence, speed, and element-count records and retained its practical engineering limitations.
change_log.reason: The reported maxima come from different demonstrations and cannot be combined into one device specification.

change_log.change: Expanded the loss comparison to include the 8.1–15.5 dB cluster, losses up to 43 dB, the +21.5 dB amplified exception, and measurement exclusions.
change_log.reason: The original range omitted substantial variation and could be mistaken for complete-system efficiency.

change_log.change: Retained the reported visible-array measurements and 2026 perspective as explicitly unverified source attributions.
change_log.reason: Neither source has retained text; missing evidence limits confidence without showing that the attributed results are false.

change_log.change: Made the effective-aperture estimate conditional on wavelength, broadside operation, uniform illumination, and an FWHM convention.
change_log.reason: A divergence value alone cannot verify physical aperture size or the absent experimental measurement.

change_log.change: Restored Tseng and colleagues' authorship and distinguished the 64-fold display experiment, 1 mm eyebox, simulated larger configuration, and scoped billion-pixel estimate.
change_log.reason: The retained review supplies these distinctions and contradicts the earlier missing-authorship note.

change_log.change: Integrated display-processing and extraction limitations, including temporal averaging and the absence of visual figure inspection.
change_log.reason: These affect interpretation and extrapolation without invalidating the documented experiment.

change_log.change: Specified proposed two-dimensional aperture and steering coverage, majority main-lobe power, complete-command settling, operating budgets, and reproducibility measurements.
change_log.reason: The original completion proposal lacked definitions needed for a convincing, repeatable combined-performance test.

change_log.change: Separated direct beam-control consequences from conditional applications and compared all supplied roster entries without merging them.
change_log.reason: Application systems and immersive displays require additional capabilities, while roster titles support only bounded conceptual comparisons.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish the latest state as of 1 November 2026 or whether any device has achieved the combined capability.
The Ye and colleagues source requires retained text to verify identity, publication details, wavelength, channel count, angular coverage, divergence convention, and transition measurements.
The claimed May 2026 APL Photonics perspective requires retained text to verify its authorship, date, DOI, and attributed integration conclusions.

The review's proposed visible-or-near-infrared completion option was not adopted as written: near-infrared operation is retained as a milestone, while visible operation is required to preserve the supplied concept identity.

Numerical angular bounds, beam-width tolerance, power budget, continuous operating duration, and environmental range remain to be chosen for a particular proposed demonstration; the supplied material establishes no consensus thresholds.
The identity and detailed requirements of historical display item 7 remain unavailable, and the other roster entries were supplied only as IDs and titles.

The 2025 review is available only through partial extractions, and the display figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review; these boundaries limit verification of details beyond the cited textual findings.

brief.title: A large light-steering surface with no moving parts
possible: Laser scanners could sweep a tight beam across a wide area without turning the surface that sends it out. The goal is a programmable surface at least a centimeter across that steers visible light sideways and vertically by coordinating the light emitted across its whole area.
why: This could improve lidar, which measures distance with laser light, communication through open air, and controlled laser delivery. A large working surface would keep the beam narrow while electronic control would rapidly change where it points.

sources.showed: This is a study of a visible-light steering array made from thin-film lithium niobate.
sources.cited_for: It concerns visible-light steering with fast electrical control.
sources.not_established: Fast changes in individual controls do not establish rapid, settled steering across a large surface.

sources.who: Weihan Xu, Qiqi Yuan, Yunhong Yang, Liangjun Lu, Jianping Chen and Linjie Zhou
sources.showed: Their review describes chip-based arrays that coordinate light emission to steer narrow beams. Different devices demonstrate large emitting areas, fast steering and large numbers of emitters.
sources.quote: integrated OPAs today can emit a diffraction-limited laser beam with sub-mrad divergence
sources.cited_for: Electronic steering already exists, alongside tradeoffs among size, speed, control complexity and useful light output.
sources.not_established: The reported achievements do not establish the required combination in a visible-light device.

sources.who: Authors of the study on optical arrays with on-chip amplification
sources.showed: Their comparison reports substantial light losses in many steering arrays and optical gain in an amplified device. The figures exclude losses where light enters from a fiber, and some count only power in the desired beam.
sources.cited_for: Useful beam power and overall optical efficiency need separate measurements.
sources.not_established: Amplification does not establish efficient, large-area visible-light steering.

sources.who: Authors of the perspective on integrated optical steering arrays
sources.showed: This is a perspective on scaling optical steering arrays through integration of electronics and light-handling components.
sources.cited_for: It discusses integration as a possible route to scalable control.
sources.not_established: A proposed integration route does not establish a working scalable device.

sources.showed: They used a fixed optical element designed through machine learning to widen the viewing field of full-color holographic images. The prototype had a small region in which the viewer’s eye could see the image.
sources.quote: we experimentally achieve 64 × étendue expansion of natural images in full color
sources.cited_for: Holographic displays face a related challenge in controlling light over a wide viewing field.
sources.not_established: The fixed optical element does not demonstrate a large, dynamically controlled beam-steering surface.

shown: Xu and colleagues describe electronic steering devices with narrow beams, fast switching and emitting areas exceeding a centimeter in one direction. These achievements come from different demonstrations; they do not establish the full combination in a visible-light surface.
missing: A large visible-light surface still needs to combine wide steering, a narrow beam, useful power and rapid updates.
Light distribution, coordinated emission and calibration still need to work together across the full surface without excessive loss or heating.
Sustained operation and repeatable performance across directions, temperatures and devices still need demonstration.

milestones.label: A large surface steers visible light widely
milestones.explanation: The surface would have to steer visible light through tens of degrees sideways and vertically, with beam width demonstrating coordinated emission across its full area. This would establish narrow beams over broad coverage.

milestones.label: Most emitted light stays in the intended beam
milestones.explanation: The main beam would have to contain more than half of all emitted light at every tested direction, with overall efficiency measured separately. This would distinguish useful steering from scattering light elsewhere.

milestones.label: The whole surface completes rapid, sustained beam updates
milestones.explanation: Complete beam commands would have to settle at least 1,000 times per second while meeting beam-quality requirements within stated power and heat budgets. This would establish usable scanning speed during sustained operation.

milestones.label: Documented results repeat across conditions and devices
milestones.explanation: Documented measurements would have to repeat across predefined directions, command changes, temperatures and devices, with independent replication where feasible. This would establish the breadth and reliability of performance.

uncertain: The steering range, acceptable beam width, power budget, operating duration and temperature range still need agreed test limits.
Simpler control architectures may reduce wiring while sending more light into unwanted directions; the practical balance remains open.

page.title: Centimeter-scale visible-light integrated optical phased array
page.definition: An integrated array of waveguide-fed emitters, supplied through on-chip optical channels, coherently uses an emitting aperture of at least 1 cm². Electronic control of their relative optical phase steers a visible-light beam in two dimensions at fixed wavelength.

goal.need: Coherent aperture size sets the angular width of a scanning beam. DARPA’s 1 cm² integration stage is 400 times the area of the visible prototype below. The infrared device also delivered 400 mW in its main beam. These passive results establish beam formation; the goal combines a larger visible emitting aperture with electronic two-axis pointing for scanning and optical links.

figures.caption: Passive silicon-nitride arrays published on 20 December 2016 in the 2017 journal issue.
figures.note: Separate passive devices; these results do not demonstrate electronic steering.

statements.body: MIT Photonic Microsystems Group, Christopher V. Poulton and Michael R. Watts
statements.quote: We are also developing visible light phased arrays

statements.body: DARPA, Modular Optical Aperture Building Blocks programme
statements.quote: integrated electronic-photonic unit cells that can be tiled together to form large-scale planar apertures.
statements.context: The programme identifies demonstration of these cells as a primary goal; the statement does not specify visible operation.

completion.title: A 1 cm² integrated aperture electronically steers a visible beam in two dimensions.
completion.criterion: One waveguide-fed integrated array coherently uses an emitting aperture of at least 1 cm². At one fixed visible wavelength, electrical phase commands steer its main beam independently in both angular coordinates without mechanical motion, with Strehl ratio >0.8 at each demonstrated direction. Strehl is measured peak far-field intensity divided by the aberration-free peak for the same wavelength, emitter geometry, amplitude illumination and total radiated power. A peer-reviewed experimental paper demonstrates the combined capability.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining DARPA MOABB’s integration area, MIT’s visible-array goal and an optical-quality convention; no outside body published this combined test.
completion.basis: Searched DARPA MOABB/SWEEPER goals, visible-OPA papers, OPA reviews and IEEE/IEC/Optica standards for a joint visible-aperture acceptance test; none was found. This fallback combines MOABB’s 1 cm² stage, MIT’s visible-array goal and the Strehl >0.8 optical convention. It sets no numerical scan-angle, efficiency, update-rate or endurance requirement.

milestones.title: A visible-light integrated array electronically steers a beam.
milestones.criterion: A waveguide-fed integrated array changes its far-field beam direction through electrical phase control at a visible wavelength. On 1 May 2025, Ye and colleagues reported a 32-channel array operating at 633 nm, with 40° steering and 0.41° full width at half maximum in the phase-controlled direction. The abstract does not state the number of devices tested. Its 12 ns rising and 14 ns falling electro-optic response edges do not establish complete-aperture command settling.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback capability stage; searches of visible-array papers and programme documents found no externally specified acceptance stage for initial visible electronic steering.

milestones.title: At least 100 optical unit cells form a 1 cm² integrated array.
milestones.criterion: Integrate at least 100 optical unit cells into a 1 cm² array, following MOABB’s published Phase 2 target. This target belongs to the programme’s tiled-aperture route and does not specify visible operation. DARPA subsequently reported that Analog Photonics met Phase II metrics and reached aperture sizes of 1 cm; that notice does not specify aperture area or unit-cell count. The agency result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, MOABB Phase 2 description published on 4 December 2015; a programme-specific integration target.
milestones.threshold_quote: a 1 cm2 array and a 10 cm2 array comprising upwards of 100 and 10,000 unit cells, respectively.

milestones.title: A visible-light integrated aperture of at least 1 cm² forms a beam with Strehl ratio >0.8.
milestones.criterion: At one fixed visible wavelength and one beam direction, a waveguide-fed integrated array uses an emitting aperture of at least 1 cm² with Strehl ratio >0.8, normalized as in the completion criterion. This establishes coherent beam formation across the enlarged aperture before two-axis steering is demonstrated. No experimental result satisfying this combined area, wavelength and optical-quality test was located.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback combining MOABB’s area stage with the published Strehl convention; no external body was found to have specified this combined visible-array milestone.

not_found: No external acceptance test combining centimeter-scale visible operation, coherent beam quality and electronic two-axis steering was located.
No common visible-array thresholds for scan angle, main-lobe power fraction, complete-command settling or operating duration were located.
No experimental demonstration satisfying the completion test or milestone m3 was located.
The supplied 2025 npj Nanophotonics review could not be reopened because the publisher redirected to an inaccessible authentication page.
The numerical Phase II acceptance metrics underlying DARPA’s reported MOABB success were not recovered.
